title: Tenali Raman, the Elephant, and the Mouse

keywords: tenali and the elephant and the mouse
full_text:
The Commander-in-Chief of the Vijayanagara army, General Veerabhadra, was excessively proud of the royal war elephant, Airavata. The beast was an immense tusker standing twelve feet tall, armored in steel plates, and trained to shatter fortress gates.
The General boasted:
'Airavata is invincible! Nothing on earth can make him turn back or tremble! He fears neither fire, nor arrows, nor lions!'

Tenali Raman smiled quietly from the pavilion:
'General, the universe is full of mysteries. The largest mountain can be moved by a hidden fault, and the mightiest giant often trembles before the smallest creature. I can make your invincible Airavata flee in terror using a creature no larger than a betel nut!'

The General laughed scornfully:
'Tenali, thou art a jester who talks nonsense! If thou canst make Airavata take a single step backward with a creature the size of a betel nut, I will surrender my jeweled sword to thee!'

The wager was accepted before King Krishnadevaraya.
The next morning, the immense war elephant was brought to the parade grounds, trumpeting fiercely, surrounded by armored cavalry.

Tenali Raman walked into the arena carrying a tiny, woven wicker box.
He walked directly in front of the towering tusker.
The elephant raised its trunk, preparing to crush the tiny man.
Tenali opened the wicker box and released a tiny, energetic grey field mouse onto the sand!

The little mouse, terrified by the thundering noise, scurried straight toward the elephant's massive front foot, seeking shelter near the shadow of its toenails.
The moment Airavata’s sensitive eyes saw the tiny creature darting toward its feet, the elephant’s ancient equine and pachyderm instinct took over:
Elephants possess an intense, instinctual terror that small creatures might crawl up their sensitive, nerve-packed trunks!

Airavata let out a shrill, panic-stricken squeal:
*‘TRUMP-EEEET!’*
The colossal beast scrambled backward, trampled the decorative flags, knocked over the commander's reviewing canopy, and bolted out of the arena at top speed, splashing into the river shallows to get away from the tiny mouse!

The entire audience erupted in roaring laughter.
General Veerabhadra stood frozen in utter mortification.
Tenali picked up the tiny mouse, placed it safely back into its wicker box, and bowed to the King:
'Maharaj, nature has designed the world with perfect balance. The mighty must never despise the weak, nor should size be mistaken for absolute invulnerability. A tiny thorn can bring down a champion, and a little mouse can rout an armored tusker!'

The King rewarded Tenali with a gold medal, and the General learned a lifelong lesson in humility.
moral: True strength does not lie in colossal size; even the mightiest fear the smallest unexpected danger.
